Six to watch

Six changes warrant closer attention because an older label hides something consequential. A machine can act, a recording can be manufactured, and a network that connects people can also limit their choices.

What counts as new?

These are editorial judgements drawn across the publications. Each trend has a primary classification. Machine agency also brings some genuinely novel capabilities, and climate adaptation is an established field entering a new phase.

New phenomenon

A capability or practice becomes possible at materially different scale or cost. Establish the capability and specify what people can now do.

New configuration

Familiar forces interact in a consequential new arrangement. The change may reverse the implications an earlier author expected.

New framing

An established force moves into a new phase or is understood through a different question. The underlying process may be decades old.

New configuration

AI becoming autonomous infrastructure

When software can take the next step

Historical roots

Naisbitt’s information society described people working with information. Earlier automation could already execute familiar routines. The additional capability is software interpreting an open-ended request, choosing tools and attempting a sequence of actions.

What has changed

Once an organisation gives an agent permissions, a generated answer can become a booking, a payment or a change to a record. Reliability across the whole sequence matters. A supervisor who checks every step may save little time, even when each step looks impressive on its own.

Why it matters

In a benefits service, drafting a letter and changing someone’s entitlement are quite different decisions about delegated authority. Whoever can inspect a decision, stop it or reverse it holds consequential power.

What to watch

Track completed cases per staff hour alongside interventions, reversals and appeals. Rising adoption with a steady checking burden would support a human–AI hybrid.

SourcesInternational AI Safety Report 2026 CSIRO · Our Future World, 2022 McKinsey · Technology Trends Outlook 2026

New phenomenon

The industrialisation of synthetic reality

A witness can be manufactured at scale

Historical roots

Fabricated stories, impersonation and manipulated photographs have long histories. EY had already identified synthetic media by 2020. The recent step is low-cost, on-demand production of convincing voices, images, video and text for different audiences.

What has changed

The cost of making another plausible account can fall faster than the cost of establishing what happened. Genuine evidence can also be dismissed as fabricated. Provenance can tell a reader about the origin and editing of a file. The claims made by its creator still need checking.

Why it matters

After a flood, a genuine appeal for help may arrive beside many plausible imitations. Verification can save resources, but a rule requiring a signed image could exclude the resident who borrowed a phone.

What to watch

Measure verification time and the share of genuine submissions rejected. Follow adoption of provenance standards and the availability of trusted, low-tech routes for witnesses.

SourcesEY · Megatrends 2020 and beyond International AI Safety Report 2026 C2PA · Content credentials explained

New configuration

Globalisation becoming geoeconomic confrontation

Interdependence becomes a source of leverage

Historical roots

The 1982 and 1990 books expected stronger global economic integration. The US National Intelligence Council was already examining its contradictions in 2004. Competition, sanctions and trade barriers each have much longer histories.

What has changed

Links built for efficiency can give governments leverage over firms and other states. A component, a payment route or a licence can become conditional on political alignment. Trade can keep growing in aggregate while particular sectors split into rival networks. This reverses an assumption about the purpose and effects of integration.

Why it matters

An aid agency can have funds and willing suppliers yet struggle to pay a local partner. The question shifts from how much crosses borders to which routes, intermediaries and permissions are available.

What to watch

Compare trade across and within blocs, alternative payment routes and concentration of critical imports. Cooperation in a particular sector could grow even during political rivalry.

SourcesFarrell & Newman · Weaponized Interdependence WEF · Global Risks Report 2026 EY · Megatrends 2020 and beyond

New framing

Climate-driven reorganisation of society

Climate becomes a question about where people can live

Historical roots

Climate research and adaptation both predate today’s lists. Earlier frameworks emphasised emissions, resource productivity and environmental damage. By 2022 CSIRO placed adaptation at the head of its framework.

What has changed

Persistent heat, water stress and flood exposure can alter where infrastructure is maintained, which homes are insurable, when outdoor work can happen and whether a community can stay together. The new phase is adaptation becoming a regular organising decision for institutions.

Why it matters

Two coastal towns with similar exposure may have very different futures. One finances defences. The other manages relocation. The value of land, tenancy rights, local consent and public finance shape who gets a viable choice.

What to watch

Follow the terms of insurance renewals, infrastructure investment and relocation agreements. Track loss at comparable levels of hazard alongside the ability of renters and owners to recover.

SourcesIPCC · Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability CSIRO · Our Future World, 2022 EIOPA · Insurance protection gaps

New configuration

Demographic bifurcation

Growing up and growing old at the same time

Historical roots

Earlier frameworks often put population growth or ageing in the headline. Both processes continue. A single global age or growth rate obscures the very different positions of countries, and of towns within them.

What has changed

In its 2024 revision the UN counted 63 countries or areas whose populations had already peaked. It expected 126 to keep growing at least through 2054. Differences in cohorts, migration and healthy longevity connect places through labour markets, education and care.

Why it matters

A shrinking district can have empty classrooms and a shortage of carers. A growing city may urgently need schools and jobs. Recruiting carers across borders can meet one community’s needs while placing pressure on another.

What to watch

Read age profiles, migration, healthy life expectancy and vacancies together. Check whether working-age growth brings secure employment and whether more years of life bring more years in good health.

SourcesUN DESA · World Population Prospects 2024 CIFS · Megatrends 2026 Sitra · Towards a new social contract

New configuration

Power moving into network infrastructure

Who can keep a network open?

Historical roots

In 1982, networks offered an alternative to organisational hierarchies. Being able to join others directly sounded decentralising. Later research asked what happens when many independent participants rely on the same intermediary.

What has changed

Cloud infrastructure, payment networks, platforms, satellites and communications links can be indispensable across borders. Operators, standards bodies and states may influence access, reliability and the terms of connection. Ownership, jurisdiction and technical control can sit in different places.

Why it matters

A community may have several internet retailers whose services all depend on one upstream provider. Counting brands would miss the shared point of failure and the practical power of whoever controls restoration.

What to watch

Ask how long it takes to switch to a genuinely independent provider, where data and permissions can travel and which services still work during an outage.

SourcesFarrell & Newman · Weaponized Interdependence CIFS · Megatrends 2026

Two further emerging themes

New framing

Trust as a scarce resource

Trust has always mattered. What changes when information is plentiful is the time and institutional capacity needed to establish whom to believe. Demand for named guarantors, trusted intermediaries or face-to-face scrutiny can rise even while content gets cheaper.

Watch the time to authenticate evidence and whose testimony is accepted without extra proof.

SourcesCSIRO · Our Future World, 2022 WEF · Global Risks Report 2026 C2PA · Content credentials explained
New configuration

An economically constrained world

Slow growth, high debts, ageing populations, investment needs and unequal ownership can coincide. A government may face greater demands for care and adaptation just as its fiscal room narrows. The configuration differs sharply across countries and over the business cycle.

Watch debt-service costs alongside real public investment, household purchasing power and the distribution of wealth.

SourcesCIFS · Megatrends 2026 Sitra · Towards a new social contract
